learn.title: Mechanisms true of every polymer
learn.intro: These tools show a fundamental polymer-science mechanism, not one material's data. Play with the sliders and inputs to find the mechanism; where a real material's data exists, you can try that too.
learn.scale.jumpHint: Select any tick on the ruler to jump to that scale.
learn.scale.station.monomer.name: Monomer & bond
learn.scale.station.monomer.sentence: The smallest thing a polymer is made of: one repeat unit and the carbon–carbon bonds tying it to the next. If that carbon carries a side group, this is where it is decided how regularly the chain will later be able to crystallise.
learn.scale.station.chain.name: Single chain
learn.scale.station.chain.sentence: Thousands of repeat units join into a chain that coils through space like a random walk. How long that chain is, and which solvent can open it up, are both settled at this scale.
learn.scale.station.lamella.name: Lamella
learn.scale.station.lamella.sentence: The chain folds back on itself many times into a crystalline sheet a few tens of nanometres thick. Every branch sticking out of the backbone gets in the way of that folding.
learn.scale.station.spherulite.name: Spherulite
learn.scale.station.spherulite.sentence: Lamellae grow outward from a nucleus into a spherulite — invisible to the naked eye, obvious under polarised light. Percent crystallinity and density are readings of this scale.
learn.scale.station.specimen.name: Specimen / part
learn.scale.station.specimen.sentence: Millions of spherulites and amorphous regions together make a part that behaves under load and under heat — no longer a molecule, a material. This is the scale at which we ask whether it is glassy or molten at a given temperature.
learn.scale.station.lifecycle.name: Life cycle
learn.scale.station.lifecycle.sentence: The finished product leaves the line, lives its life, and one day has to be recycled, burned or buried. The largest scale a molecular decision ever reaches.
learn.scale.station.lifecycle.gap: The life-cycle / CO₂ tool is not built. 'Carbon footprint (virgin resin)' (co2_footprint_virgin) is a registered property in the data model, but no material currently has a value recorded for it — this database holds no measured emissions or production-energy data, and producing a number that looks like an LCA result is precisely what this project exists to prevent.
learn.state.title: State simulator
learn.state.intro: Move the sample's temperature and watch a polymer pass from rigid glass, through a rubbery or semi-crystalline plateau, into melt flow, and finally thermal degradation.
learn.state.materialLabel: Seed with a real material's data (optional)
learn.state.materialLoading: Looking for materials with a glass-transition value…
learn.state.illustrativeNote: These numbers are an illustrative example, not measured data for a real material. Pick a material above to see real thresholds.
learn.state.boundNote: Automatically set to {material}'s real data, since you arrived from its datasheet page.
learn.state.boundNoDataNote: {material} has no glass transition temperature (Tg) on record in this database, so the illustrative example below is shown instead.
learn.state.phase.glass.title: Glassy, rigid state
learn.state.phase.glass.desc: Below the glass transition (Tg), chain segments barely move and the amorphous regions are frozen in place — the material behaves rigid, hard and brittle.
learn.state.phase.rubber.title: Semi-crystalline / rubbery state
learn.state.phase.rubber.desc: Above Tg, chains in the amorphous regions gain enough energy for segmental motion, but the remaining crystallites still hold the material's mechanical stability — usually the polymer's main service range.
learn.state.phase.meltAmorphous.title: Rubbery / viscoelastic melt flow
learn.state.phase.meltAmorphous.desc: Because this polymer is fully amorphous, there is no crystalline melt phase — it moves straight from glassy into viscoelastic flow, ready for processing.
learn.state.phase.meltCrystalline.title: Viscous melt flow
learn.state.phase.meltCrystalline.desc: The sample has passed its crystalline melting point (Tm). Crystallites have fully opened into a viscoelastic fluid ready for extrusion, injection or blow moulding.
learn.state.phase.burn.title: Thermal degradation
learn.state.phase.burn.desc: The sample has passed its thermal degradation threshold (Td). Thermal energy now exceeds the chain's bond energy, causing scission, depolymerisation and a sharp drop in molecular weight.
learn.dp.title: Degree-of-polymerization calculator
learn.dp.intro: The number-average degree of polymerization (DPn) is the average count of monomer units in a chain. Change the values to see how it relates to weight-average molar mass (Mw) and the polydispersity index (PDI).
learn.dp.materialLabel: Seed with a real material's data (optional)
learn.dp.materialLoading: Looking for materials with an Mn value…
learn.dp.boundNote: Automatically set to {material}'s real data, since you arrived from its datasheet page.
learn.dp.boundNoDataNote: {material} does not have both Mn and the repeat unit's molar mass on record in this database, so the default values below stay editable instead.
learn.branching.title: Chain-branching simulator
learn.branching.intro: Branching is the defining axis of the polyethylenes. Pick an architecture to see how it changes chain packing — and, through packing, crystallinity and density. Only shown for the polyolefin family, where this is the mechanism that actually separates HDPE, LDPE and LLDPE.
learn.branching.architecture.linear.desc: Coordination-catalysed, low-pressure polymerisation gives an essentially unbranched backbone. Chains pack tightly into a dense crystal lattice.
learn.branching.architecture.longChainBr: High-pressure, free-radical polymerisation causes intramolecular chain transfer ("backbiting"), producing a few long, irregular branches. They disrupt packing badly.
learn.branching.architecture.shortChainB: A deliberate alpha-olefin comonomer (butene, hexene or octene) is copolymerised in — NOT long-chain branching, a different route entirely — giving many short, regular branches and an intermediate, more controlled disruption of packing.
learn.branching.illustrativeNote: These bars show the direction and rough size of the effect, not a number for any specific material — more branching lowers packing, crystallinity and density, but the exact values differ by grade and are never read off a slider.
learn.branching.materialLabel: Compare with a real polyolefin's data (optional)
learn.branching.ppNote: Branching also matters for PP, as comonomer content and copolymer architecture — but the three-way HDPE/LDPE/LLDPE contrast above is the core mechanism this tool teaches.
learn.branching.boundNote: {material}, from its datasheet page, was selected below for comparison with real data.
learn.branching.boundArchitectureNote: Chain architecture was automatically selected based on {material}'s recorded chain type.
learn.tacticity.title: Tacticity simulator
learn.tacticity.intro: Tacticity is the arrangement of a side group along the chain — and it only exists where the backbone carbon has one to arrange. Click the side groups below to rearrange them, or pick a preset, and see how the arrangement changes crystallinity and melting behaviour. Only shown for polymers with a substituted, stereogenic carbon (PP, ABS, PS, PVC, PMMA) — never for the polyethylenes, whose symmetric ethylene monomer has no side group to arrange in the first place.
learn.tacticity.mode.atactic.label: Atactic
learn.tacticity.mode.atactic.desc: Side groups point randomly to either side. No long-range regularity, so chains cannot pack into a crystal lattice — the polymer is amorphous.
learn.tacticity.mode.isotactic.label: Isotactic
learn.tacticity.mode.isotactic.desc: Every side group points to the same side. The regular repeat lets chains fold into a helix and pack into a semi-crystalline structure.
learn.tacticity.mode.syndiotactic.label: Syndiotactic
learn.tacticity.mode.syndiotactic.desc: Side groups alternate sides strictly. Also regular — often the most readily crystallised of the three for a given polymer.
learn.tacticity.chainHint: Click a side group to flip it
learn.tacticity.illustrativeNote: These are directional trends, not measured values for any specific material — the exact crystallinity and Tm a stereoregular grade reaches depend on catalyst, molecular weight and processing, and are never read off this diagram.
learn.tacticity.materialLoading: Looking for materials with a stereogenic backbone…

learn.hansen.title: Hansen solubility space
learn.hansen.intro: A rotatable 3D view of Hansen solubility space (dispersion, polar, hydrogen-bonding). Pick as many solvents as you want to see them positioned against the polymer this page is dedicated to — the full solvent list is not plotted here by default.
learn.hansen.noSolvents: No solvent data is loaded yet — the solvent table is still being populated. This chart will fill in as solvents are added.
learn.hansen.noPolymerNote: No material in this database currently has all three Hansen parameters recorded, so no polymer marker can be shown yet — you can still add and rotate solvents above.
learn.hansen.boundNote: Showing {material}'s position, linked from its datasheet page.
learn.hansen.boundNoHansenNote: {material} does not yet have all three Hansen parameters recorded in this database, so it can't be positioned on this chart.
learn.hansen.selectedUncited: {material}'s Hansen parameters are not yet backed by a citation in this database.
learn.hansen.noRoNote: No published interaction radius (Ro) is linked to {material} in this database, so it is shown as a single point rather than a solubility sphere — a radius is never invented to fill that gap.
learn.hansen.roNote: {material}'s position and its solubility sphere both come from a published Hansen correlation, with an interaction radius Ro of {ro} MPa^0.5, cited to the printed handbook page.
learn.hansen.roUncited: {material}'s position and its solubility sphere come from a Hansen correlation with an interaction radius Ro of {ro} MPa^0.5, which is not yet backed by a citation in this database.
learn.hansen.sphereNote: The sphere is drawn at that recorded Ro and at no other radius. Because all three axes share one scale, it is a true circle at every rotation: its size on screen never changes as you rotate, only its position.
learn.hansen.redLegend: Solvent fill — RED, the Hansen distance divided by the radius (Ra ÷ Ro)
learn.hansen.redGood: RED below 0.9 — inside the sphere, a likely solvent (filled dot)
learn.hansen.redBoundary: RED between 0.9 and 1.1 — on the sphere's surface, too close to call (part-filled dot)
learn.hansen.redPoor: RED above 1.1 — outside the sphere, unlikely to dissolve it (open ring)
learn.hansen.redBoundaryNote: The 0.9–1.1 band is not a stylistic choice. Published Ro values are quoted to one decimal on a scale of roughly 5 to 15 and shift by several percent when refitted against a different set of solvents, so a narrower band would colour a solvent on a difference smaller than the radius's own precision. RED is a guide to closeness in solubility space, not a prediction of dissolution.
learn.hansen.metricNote: All three axes now share one scale, and the dispersion axis is drawn at 2δD — the standard Hansen convention. Because of that, straight-line distance on screen IS the Hansen distance Ra, at every rotation, so the “closest solvents” list and the picture always agree.
learn.hansen.axisDWeightNote: The dispersion axis is plotted as 2δD, so its tick labels are δD itself, not the doubled value.
learn.hansen.viewNote: Fitting to your selection only zooms the same cube — the scale stays equal on all three axes, so distances still mean Ra.
learn.hansen.rotateHint: Drag to rotate the scene, scroll to zoom.
learn.hansen.unitNote: A solvent dot's outline carries its provenance: a solid outline means a recorded citation, a dashed outline means not yet cited. When a solubility sphere is shown, the fill colour carries RED instead (see the key above); with no sphere the fill falls back to that same provenance meaning — sage for cited, grey for not. The larger marker is the selected polymer's own position.
learn.hansen.searchHint: Type at least 2 characters — the full 1,180-solvent list isn't shown here; browse all of it on the Solvents page.
learn.hansen.selectedEmpty: No solvents selected yet. Search above, or add from the closest matches below once a polymer is shown.
learn.hansen.raNote: Ra is the Hansen distance between each solvent and the selected polymer — smaller means a closer match in solubility space, not a guarantee of dissolution.
learn.chain.title: Chain Coil — 2D Random Walk
learn.chain.intro: A polymer chain coils through space like a random walk: each repeat unit turns in a random direction. Change the degree of polymerisation (DP) to watch the chain become a denser coil — the Rg ∝ √N relationship, made visible.
learn.chain.unitNote: Distances are reported in bond lengths (a dimensionless unit, roughly one C–C bond), not nanometres — this is an idealised, fully free-jointed chain with no bond-angle constraint or excluded volume, so converting it precisely to nanometres for a real material would be an invented claim.
learn.chain.varianceNote: Rg ∝ √N is a statistical average over many chains, not a smooth curve for one specific chain — this single random path can grow more slowly over some DP range, which is real behaviour, not an error.
learn.chain.boundNote: The DP slider was seeded from {material}'s real Mn and repeat-unit molar mass.
learn.chain.boundNoDataNote: {material} does not have both Mn and the repeat unit's molar mass on record, so the slider starts from its default value.

learn.map.offcurve.chainCoil.label: Chain coil — random walk
learn.map.offcurve.chainCoil.hint: Not temperature-dependent — the chain's statistical geometry changes with DP, not with temperature.
learn.map.offcurve.tacticity.label: Tacticity simulator
learn.map.offcurve.tacticity.hint: Not temperature-dependent — the spatial arrangement at each stereocentre is set during polymerisation and stays fixed.
learn.map.phase.glass.title: Glassy
learn.map.phase.glass.desc: Below Tg the chains are effectively frozen: only small vibrations happen, large-scale chain motion is switched off — hard and brittle.
learn.map.phase.rubber.title: Semicrystalline plateau
learn.map.phase.rubber.desc: The amorphous regions have softened, but the crystallites are still standing; they hold the modulus up until close to Tm.
learn.map.phase.meltAmorphous.title: Flow (past Tg)
learn.map.phase.meltAmorphous.desc: This material has no crystallites, so nothing holds the modulus up: right past Tg the chains slide freely past each other and the material begins to flow.
learn.map.phase.meltCrystalline.title: Melt
learn.map.phase.meltCrystalline.desc: Above Tm the crystallites have melted, the chains slide freely past each other and the material flows — the extrusion and injection-moulding region.
learn.map.phase.burn.title: Thermal degradation
learn.map.phase.burn.desc: Above this temperature the backbone bonds break. This is no longer a process, it is irreversible damage.
learn.graph.title: The causal graph of polymer properties
learn.graph.intro: Polymer properties are not independent of one another: chain branching affects crystallinity, crystallinity affects density and stiffness, and together these determine which application the material actually suits. Drag one of the three input nodes and watch the effect flow downstream.
learn.graph.dragHint: Drag the input nodes vertically; the keyboard works too — focus a node and press the Up/Down arrow keys or Home/End.

learn.graph.panelNote: Dragging any of the three input nodes updates this column and the diagram using this page's own simple, illustrative relations — independent of any measured value shown alongside it.
learn.graph.rowInfo.withMeasured: The measured value ({value} {unit}) is from {material}'s datasheet and its status is "{status}". The "illustrative trend" is a separate number: it only shows the direction this property responds to the inputs, not a quantitative prediction for {material}.

learn.graph.rowInfo.noMaterial: No material is selected. The "illustrative trend" only shows which direction dragging the inputs moves this property — independent of any specific material, and with no real physical unit.
learn.graph.closingNote: This diagram is not a validated model. Each edge's direction (↑/↓) comes from established polymer science, but the exact slope of each relation and every node's "illustrative trend" are this page's own construction for teaching — a unitless number, not a measurement. The only thing that genuinely comes from the datasheet is each property's measured value for the selected material, shown with the same provenance mark it carries there.
learn.graph.outcomes.film.copy: Higher molecular weight means the melt has enough strength to hold a blown-film bubble without tearing.
learn.graph.outcomes.inj.copy: Lower molecular weight means a more fluid melt — suited to filling a mould quickly during injection.
learn.graph.outcomes.cable.copy: Lower density means a larger amorphous fraction and better flexibility for cable insulation.
learn.graph.relationsIntro: The same diagram drawn above, listed here as plain sentences for screen readers and keyboard navigation — each row is one edge of the graph.
